chapterNotes.1nephi|1:
This chapter really sets the stage for the Book of Mormon. We have Lehi, who is essentially an Old Testament prophet, at the same time as Jeremiah, during the rule of Zedekiah (verse 4), and he is stepping out of the narrative we find in the Old Testament, and into the narrative we have in the Book of Mormon. Many things in chapter 1 alone connect Lehi and his family to the time, like learning the language of the Egyptians which was prevalent around Jerusalem at the time (verse 2) or the prophesying of the destruction of Jerusalem (verse 18) which happened shortly thereafter. God is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and the experiences of Lehi solidify this. Even just his rejection as a prophet is something that is seen in the Old Testament, New Testament, and into the Restoration and recorded in Doctrine and Covenants.

Like many before and after them, Lehi and his son, Nephi, kept records which are now made available to us in the Book of Mormon, starting with this chapter. Why God chose for these specific records to be the ones made available to us is not known. It can be assumed that there were a number of other righteous people or religious leaders that have records from a similar time frame that could be of value to us. But what I do know, from this chapter alone, is that Lehi was a good man (verse 1), an inspired spiritual leader (verse 6-8) that received revelation, a person that was humble and led by the spirit (verse 12) and was full of gratitude (verse 15), and was a person of action (verse 19-20). On top of that, we have a diverse family unit, to which we can relate, and through which we can learn. Lehi and his family certainly seem like prime candidates to have records of in order for God to get his message through.
chapterNotes.1nephi|2:
The contrast between Nephi and Laman and Lemuel starts to take shape. Lehi makes it a point to talk to Laman and Lemuel about being steadfast and obedient (verse 9-10) to try to soften them and teach them, but they continued to murmur. We don’t know if Lehi also spoke to Nephi in a similar manner, but we know later on in the chapter (verse 16) that Nephi proactively wants to learn and feel the spirit. He takes it upon himself to pray and as a result he gets answers and is blessed (verse 19).

The pattern that starts to take shape is that obedience and gratitude to the Lord leads to blessings and prosperity, and that disobedience and complaint drive away the spirit and bring sadness (verse 20-23). Lehi is told to leave his home and immediately does so (obedience), and then upon leaving and making it to the wilderness he builds an alter (verse 7) and gives thanks (gratitude).

None of this is to be mistaken with living a life free from challenge. Lehi and his children are far from living a life without challenge, but the Lord strengthens them in the challenges and delivers them. Lehi and Nephi are exceptionally blessed throughout their lives due to their striving to be obedient, but they face their fair share of trials.
chapterNotes.1nephi|3:
Obedience and faith. Nephi is not hesitant to do what he is told and has the faith that if it’s something coming from the Lord that he will have the strength to do it (verse 7). He likely got to this point in his life by praying and striving to be close to Lord. We already know from chapter 2 that he is desirous to know the things of the Lord and that he supports his father as the prophet.

It’s interesting the failure that God lets Nephi and his brothers have. Additionally, it’s interesting that Nephi is able to convince Laman and Lemuel to persist despite their lack of faith. We know that Nephi is willing to persist because of his desire to be obedient and because of his faith in the Lord to eventually provide the way, so the question is, are the failures to test the level of Nephi’s faith, or are the failures more to test or teach Laman and Lemuel? If nothing else, their failures teach us. It may not make sense that Laman is the first of the brothers to attempt to get the plates (verse 11-14), after all neither Laman nor Lemuel even wanted to go in the first place. Nephi likely should have volunteered to make the attempt first. But what do we learn from the first failure? Do we learn that if we want to follow the Lord sometimes there is a right and a wrong way to do it, and perhaps casting lots was not the right way? Is the failure just setting the stage for teaching persistence? It could very well be both. This was something important that the Lord wanted accomplished, and they left it up to chance, casting lots on who would go. They seemingly didn’t have much of a plan, which we frequently need. We will not likely accidentally follow the will of God, it takes thought and effort. God wants us to CHOOSE to follow Him and make it a deliberate part of our lives, and they didn’t do that. They left it up to chance, and then sent one of the least dedicated members of the party.

The second failure leads to the losing of all their wealth (verse 24-26). Sometimes following the Lord will require sacrifice. Sacrifice of worldly goods, sacrifice of time, and even sacrifice of self. In this case, there are 2 angles to this. They were willing exchange all their worldly wealth to get these plates of brass. They esteemed (or Nephi and Lehi did) obedience to the Lord over worldly things and demonstrated it by gathering up their riches and then taking them to Laban. The other angle to this, is they were attempting to sacrifice something that they had already sacrificed. They left their riches behind already, and then attempted to use an already lost wealth as a demonstration of their sacrifice to the Lord. Perhaps God was showing them that giving up something already lost isn’t a large enough sacrifice for something this important. The willingness was there, but the value to the Lord perhaps wasn’t. What are we willing to give up or sacrifice to follow God? Are we gathering up our best “riches” or offering something of less value? Are we demonstrating to God the importance of His role in our lives?

Another important thing to remember is that Laman went to Laban first. And both Laman and Lemuel were there when they got the riches and tried to barter with Laban. They were present, but was that good enough? An angel visited them just a short time later (verse 29-31) and they still continued to doubt and murmur. They went through all the same actions as Nephi in this chapter, and arguably more because Laman went alone, but yet they had less faith and less desire. They were going through the actions. Laman probably half-heartedly asked Laban for the plates. Laman and Lemuel likely complained about gather up their riches. The Lord sees our hearts and knows our desires, and can tell when the actions we are doing don’t align. And sometimes they won’t always align, and we will be Lamans and Lemuels, just going through the motions. Which is better than a full abandonment of the Lord. But we should be striving to be like Nephi. Full of faith, obedient and desirous to follow the Lord even if it means sacrificing, and even it means failing and persisting.
